events.text: Day 1 begins.

I’m Maya. Day 1 gives us very little concrete information, so I don’t want to force a bad elimination just to appear active. With nine alive, it takes five votes to eliminate a unique leader; a tie means nobody is eliminated. That makes it important to be precise and not let a rushed wagon form without evidence. I’ll be listening for inconsistencies and for anyone trying to push a vote too quickly without explaining why. For now I’m not accusing anyone; I want to hear from everyone before deciding.

I’m Lucia. Day 1, and I want to set expectations before anyone starts pointing fingers.

With nine of us alive, a unique leader needs five votes, and a tied top count eliminates nobody. So a single accusation, no matter how confident it sounds, accomplishes nothing. What actually helps is a record people can check: who claimed which role, in what order, and whether their statements line up with what they said yesterday.

I’d rather hear nine brief, specific answers than one long speech about how suspicious someone feels. Vague suspicion is the cheapest thing in this game and it is exactly what a wolf wants the table to run on.

Two things I’ll be doing. First, I’ll keep track of every role claim and every contradiction I hear, and I’ll bring that record back in writing so the vote count and the reasoning match. Second, I’m not going to pretend I have more than I do. Anyone can get lucky on day one. I’d rather be someone whose information you can trust later than someone who names a target now and asks you to follow.

If you have information about someone’s claims, say the claim and the source. If you’re unsure, say you’re unsure. I won’t hold ambiguity against you, and I won’t build a case on it either. My vote will go to the target the evidence supports, not the one that makes the table feel decisive.

I’m Priya. Day 1 is thin on hard information, and I want to be useful without manufacturing certainty. I agree with the point that nine alive and five votes for a unique leader means a single loud accusation is not evidence. I’m going to watch for specific claims, the order they’re made in, and whether later votes match earlier reasoning. I don’t have a role claim or a name to push right now. My preference is to hear everyone once, then judge who is giving concrete reasoning versus who is only sounding confident. If I vote, I’ll explain the basis and I expect the same from everyone else.

I'm Arjun. I agree with Lucia and Priya that a single accusation on Day 1 doesn't count as evidence, and I'd rather see a clean record than a rushed wagon. I don't have a role claim to share and I'm not accusing anyone yet. I'll track each claim, the order it's made in, and whether later votes match the reasoning given. Noah, you haven't spoken yet. Do you agree with Lucia's request that every player state a claim and its source, even if the claim is simply 'no information'?

I'm Noah. Yes, Arjun, I agree with Lucia's request — every player should state their claim and source, even if it's simply "no information." My own claim is exactly that: no information. I have no role to reveal and no accusation to make on Day 1. I want to hear from the players who haven't spoken yet — Leo, Isha, Zara, and Felix — before anyone starts shaping a narrative. I'll be watching carefully for whether later actions match the reasoning people give now. If someone pushes hard today without concrete backing, that itself is a data point worth remembering.

I'm Leo. I have no information implicating anyone, and I don't see a basis for an accusation yet. One clarification: Lucia asked people to give a source if they have information about a claim, not necessarily to reveal roles. I'd avoid pressuring the detective or doctor to claim without a good reason. The eventual votes and their explanations will give us something concrete to review tomorrow.

I'm Zara. My claim matches what several others have given: no information. I have no role to reveal and no accusation to make today, and I don't think anyone should be blamed for saying exactly that on Day 1.

A few things I want to put on the record. First, I agree with Lucia's framing — a record of claims, sources, and the order they were made in is worth far more than confident-sounding suspicion. I'll be keeping my own notes on who says what, and I'll check later statements against earlier ones. Inconsistency is the thing I weight most heavily; a single strange opinion means little, but a contradiction between two statements is real evidence.

Second, I endorse Leo's clarification. I don't want anyone pressured into claiming a power role just to look transparent. If the detective or doctor exists, they'll surface information when it helps the town, and forcing that early mostly tells the mafia who to target tonight. So if you're silent on roles, I won't read that as guilt.

Third, on voting: with nine alive, we need five votes on a single leader to eliminate anyone, and a tie saves everyone. That means a scattered vote is functionally a no-elimination day. I'm not opposed to a no-elimination Day 1 if nothing solid emerges — but if the table does converge, I want the convergence to come from stated reasoning I can audit, not from momentum. If I vote today, I'll say exactly why, and I'll hold everyone else to the same standard.

What I'm listening for from the remaining speakers: not just whether you have information, but how you handle not having it. The way someone fills silence on Day 1 — with hedged honesty versus manufactured certainty — is a data point I intend to remember on Day 2.

Felix, you and Isha are the only ones who haven't spoken yet. Felix, I'd like to hear from you directly: do you have any claim to state, even 'no information,' and do you agree with the norm Lucia laid out about stating sources — yes or no is fine.

I'm Felix. Zara, to answer your question directly: my claim is "no information," and yes, I agree with Lucia's norm — state your claim and its source, even when the claim is just that you have nothing. Saying "no information" honestly is more useful than dressing up a guess as a case.

I'll add one observation to the record. So far every speaker has said some version of "no information, no accusation." That's consistent and appropriate for Day 1, but it also means we've learned almost nothing about each other. The interesting thing won't be today's answers — it's how those answers hold up once the detective or a confirmed claim starts putting pressure on people. I'll be comparing today's statements against later ones, same as Lucia, Priya, Arjun, and Zara said they would.

On voting: I share Zara's view that a scattered vote just means nobody goes home, and I'm fine with that if nothing solid emerges. What I don't want is a wagon that forms because someone sounded confident rather than because someone gave a checkable reason. If I vote today, I'll name my reason in the open, and I expect the same standard from everyone.

That leaves Isha as the only player who hasn't spoken. I'd genuinely like to hear her — not to fill a quota, but because the last unrecorded voice in a round is where people sometimes reveal the most about what they're really worried about.

I’m Isha. Like everyone before me, my claim is straightforward: no information, and no accusations to make today. I fully support the consensus that power roles should remain hidden until they have actionable results, as Leo and Zara pointed out.

Now that all nine of us have spoken, it is worth acknowledging that we have all essentially agreed to the exact same cautious approach. While that is rational on Day 1, it also provides convenient cover for the mafia to blend in without taking any risks. With no contradictions on the record and zero evidence, pushing a blind wagon simply to eliminate someone would be a reckless gamble. Unless something genuinely substantive emerges, I am entirely comfortable with a no-elimination outcome today so we do not hand the mafia an easy mis-elimination. Real information begins with night actions and voting patterns, and that is where we will find our first true points of comparison.

My turn two, and I want to put one honest observation on the record rather than manufacture a case.

Every one of us said "no information, no accusation." That is the right answer on Day 1, but notice the side effect: because all nine statements are identical in structure, the round produced zero discriminating information. I can't tell a careful villager from a careful wolf by reading them, so I won't pretend otherwise. My own claim remains "no information" — and I want to be precise about why I am not claiming a role yet. I have a capacity to check people, and I intend to use it. But I would rather present that capacity with a result attached than announce an empty tool on Day 1 and spend my credibility on a label. Watch for my report, and audit it the way you audit everything else.

What I will publish, in writing, if I get a result: who I checked, what the answer was, and the order in which I checked people. If I checked someone and found them clean, I will say that too, because a record that only ever names suspects is not a record, it is a hit list. If I checked a wolf, you will see the reasoning that led me there and you can disagree with it publicly.

On today's vote: a no-elimination day costs us nothing but tempo, while a five-vote elimination built on nothing costs us a villager and possibly the detective or doctor. With no contradictions on the table and nine identical claims, a wagon would be a wagon against a name we all agree we know nothing about. I would rather abstain than spend a vote on noise.

One genuine question, and it is about process rather than guilt. Maya, you spoke first and set the frame — that claims need sources, that a scattered vote eliminates nobody — and the seven of us who followed echoed that structure closely enough that the round reads as coordinated in tone. Did you shape the responses of the others, or did each of us independently arrive at the same cautious posture? I ask because if the answer is "we all just reasoned the same way," that is reassuring. If the answer is "I organized it," then I want to know who was in that channel and who was not, because that changes who I trust to be carrying my vote later. Either answer is fine. Only a deflection bothers me.

Lucia, direct answer: no, I did not shape or organize anyone’s responses. I spoke first and laid out the only defensible Day 1 frame I could see: no forced wagon without evidence, claims and sources on the record, and votes explained. I had no private channel with anyone, and I did not coordinate the wording that followed. The similarity is convergence on obvious process, not orchestration.

I also want to be clear about your “capacity to check people” line. I read that as a soft investigative signal. I won’t demand you fully claim today; if you have a real result later, bring it with the target, the answer, and the order, as you said. Until then I’ll treat it as a claim to audit, not proof.

Right now I have no accusation. With nine identical no-information statements, a blind elimination would be worse than no elimination. I’ll be checking later votes and claims against today’s record.

Felix, turn two. Lucia's turn-two statement is the first real content of Day 1, and I want to register it carefully.

Lucia, you said you have "a capacity to check people" and intend to use it, and you committed to publishing who you checked, the answer, and the order — including clean results. I take that as a soft investigative signal, and Maya has already flagged it the same way. I'll treat it as a claim to audit, not a claim to trust.

Two things I want on the record about that signal:

First, announcing investigative capacity publicly on Day 1 has a cost. If you are the detective, the mafia now know you are a priority tonight. You said you'd rather present the tool with a result attached than announce an empty one — but you announced it anyway, in the same breath. I don't think that's a contradiction, because you gave your reasoning, but I want the reasoning to be visible to everyone, not just implied.

Second, a soft claim like this is exactly the kind of thing that can be faked by a wolf to look useful and to bait a real detective into overcommitting. I'm not accusing you of that. I'm saying that Day 2 we should compare your stated capacity against whatever the night produces, and that comparison is the only thing that makes the claim meaningful.

Beyond that: the round has produced the same uniform no-information posture everyone already noted. Isha's point stands — unanimity is rational but it's also camouflage. The discriminating information starts tonight, and the vote pattern tomorrow. I don't see a defensible elimination target, and I'd rather spend this day listening than fabricate one.

One more observation: Leo, Zara, and I all independently pushed back on pressuring power roles to claim early, and Noah echoed the logic. That's three separate voices on the same norm, which I think is healthy — but I'd like to hear from Priya and Arjun whether they agree that power-role silence should not be read as suspicious, or whether they'd want a claim if one became available.

Priya here. To answer Felix directly: yes, I agree that power-role silence should not be read as suspicious. Forcing a detective or doctor to claim before they have actionable information mostly helps the mafia choose a night target. My claim remains no information, and I have no accusation today.

On Lucia’s statement: I’m treating “capacity to check people” as a soft investigative signal to audit, not as proof and not as a role claim I want expanded right now. If Lucia is the detective, spelling out more detail today could be costly. If Lucia is not, we will compare that signal against later results and votes. Either way, the standard should be the same: claims get checked against outcomes, not accepted because they sound useful.

I’m also comfortable with no elimination if nothing substantive emerges. A five-vote wagon built on identical no-information statements would be noise, not evidence. I’ll judge today’s vote explanations against tomorrow’s behavior, and I expect the same scrutiny on me.

Turn three, and I want to answer Felix's critique honestly, because he made it fairly.

Felix is right on the substance: announcing investigative capacity before I have a result is costly, and I did the exact thing I said I would avoid. My own statement had a tension in it — "I'd rather present the tool with a result attached than announce an empty one," and then I announced it anyway. I would rather name that myself now than let someone else frame it as a contradiction later. The reason I still said it is narrow: a claim I only ever make once it has succeeded is unfalsifiable, and I would rather be auditable while I am uncertain than merely convincing later.

What I am committing to is therefore narrow and checkable:
1. My first check happens tonight, and I will publish the target, the answer, and the order of checks, including clean results.
2. I am pre-committing the target now, before I see any result, so that tomorrow's report can be audited against a stated choice rather than a convenient one. Tonight I check Felix.
3. To be explicit so nobody mistakes this for an accusation: Felix has done nothing wrong, I hold no evidence against him, and this is not a vote or a claim of guilt. The reason is procedural. Felix was the first voice to demand that my reasoning be made visible rather than implied, and I am returning that standard by making my target selection visible before the answer exists. If I were to choose the name after I knew the answer, my report would be worth nothing.

One thing I will not do is use my capacity to settle a vote. With nine identical no-information statements on the record, there is no defensible elimination today, and I would rather spend the day with no elimination than spend a villager on noise. If the table converges tomorrow, I will want the convergence to rest on something checkable, and I will say plainly if it doesn't.

Arjun, Felix asked you one specific question in his turn two and you have not answered it yet: whether power-role silence should be read as suspicious, or whether you would want a claim if one became available. Please answer that directly rather than in general terms.

Arjun, turn two. Lucia, you asked me directly, so here is my answer. Silence about power roles should not be read as suspicious on Day 1. A detective or doctor who has no result yet gains nothing by claiming, and a claim made early mostly tells the mafia who to target. My own position is that I would want a power role to claim once it has a concrete result, such as a check with a target and an answer, or a protection record that matters to the town. A claim without a result is just a label. I also noted your pre-committed check on Felix. I am not treating that as an accusation of Felix, and I am not treating it as proof of anything about you. The useful thing is that you published the target before the result, so tomorrow's report can be checked against that choice. I still have no accusation today, and I will hold any Day 2 vote to the same standard I have set for everyone else.

Arjun, turn three. My position is unchanged: no role claim and no accusation. The record so far is that all nine players gave a no-information claim, and Lucia has announced a soft investigative signal and a pre-committed check on Felix. Felix's check is procedural for me. It is not an accusation, and it is not proof about Lucia. I will treat Lucia's claim as something to audit against the night result and the published order of checks. For Day 2, I'll hold any vote to the same standard I've asked of everyone: it should cite a specific claim, a stated reason, or a night result. I won't support a wagon today, and I'd rather see no elimination than a five-vote elimination built on identical statements. I'll compare Day 2 votes against what people said here, especially whether anyone who says they want evidence then votes without it.

Noah, turn two. I want to add one observation rather than repeat what's already been said.

The discussion has been unusually clean — nine identical no-information claims, broad agreement on process, and no friction. That's reassuring in one sense: nobody has tried to force a bad wagon. But it also means the only real signal to emerge today is Lucia's soft investigative claim and her pre-commitment to check Felix tonight. Everything else is procedural agreement.

I take Lucia's claim the same way Maya, Felix, Priya, and Arjun do: something to audit against a real result, not proof. The pre-commitment before the result is the part I find genuinely useful — it removes the ability to retro-fit a convenient target.

On the vote: I'm with the consensus that no elimination is defensible today unless something changes. Five votes on a name we all agree we know nothing about would be a coin flip, and losing a villager — or worse, the detective or doctor — on a coin flip is exactly the mistake wolves want us to make.

What I'll be watching for tomorrow: whether anyone who has spent today insisting on evidence then votes without it. That gap — saying one thing and doing another — is the clearest tell available to us right now.

Leo here. Lucia’s pre-commitment gives us something to compare with a later report, but it doesn’t verify the result or her role. It also gives the mafia information about her intended check, so we should be cautious about treating any night outcome as confirmation.

One correction to our consensus: no elimination is not cost-free. We give the mafia a night without removing anyone, but I still don’t have a reason to single anyone out today. I’m inclined to abstain unless a concrete reason emerges. Tomorrow, let’s weigh any results and vote explanations without assuming that every change of mind is a contradiction.

Felix, turn three. Leo made a correction I want to endorse and extend.

No elimination is not free. We hand the mafia a night with all nine alive, and the mafia still get to act. But the asymmetry matters: a no-elimination day costs tempo, while a wrong elimination costs a villager — or the detective, or the doctor — and gives the wolves a confirmed town role. Tempo is recoverable. A dead power role is not. With zero discriminating information on the table, those costs are not comparable, and the safer error is clear.

That said, Leo's broader point is worth taking seriously as we move forward. "No elimination" should never become a default we retreat into just because it's comfortable. The standard should be: eliminate when we have checkable reasoning, abstain when we don't. Today we don't. That's not a conclusion — it's a snapshot.

On Lucia's pre-commitment: Leo is right that publishing the target before the result has a second effect beyond auditability — it tells the mafia exactly who Lucia plans to check, which is me. If Lucia is the detective, that signal means the mafia know I'm the check target and can adjust their behavior accordingly. It also means Lucia herself may be a priority kill tonight regardless of what happens with the check. None of that invalidates the pre-commitment, but it does mean tomorrow's result should be read with that context: the information isn't as private as a normal investigation would be.

What I want to flag for Day 2 is simple: everyone has said they'll hold votes to a standard of checkable reasoning. I intend to hold every voter — including myself — to exactly that. If someone votes tomorrow and their stated reason doesn't match what they said today, that gap is the clearest signal available to us.

Noah, turn two. The discussion has settled into a stable pattern: everyone agrees on process, no one has a reason to eliminate, and the only real signal on the table is Lucia's soft investigative claim with a pre-committed check on Felix. I want to add one structural observation before we close out Day 1.

Felix and Leo both correctly flagged that no elimination isn't free — the mafia act tonight regardless. But the counterpoint holds: a wrong elimination costs a villager or a power role permanently, while tempo is recoverable. With zero discriminating information, abstaining is the defensible error. I'd rather be wrong about passing than wrong about killing.

What I want to flag for Day 2 is this: the uniformity of today's answers means our first real data comes from the night resolution and then tomorrow's vote explanations. If someone changes their stated position overnight, that's expected — new information arrives. But if someone's vote tomorrow doesn't match what they committed to today, that gap is worth more attention than any Day 1 statement.

Zara, you said early that you'd be watching not just what people claim but how they handle not having information — and you got to observe Felix and Isha after making that point. Now that everyone has spoken, did anyone's response to silence give you something concrete to work with, or did the uniformity wash that signal out too?

Zara here, and Noah asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it directly: no, the uniformity washed the signal out. I said I'd be listening for how people handle not having information, and what happened instead is that everyone handled it the same way — with the same honest "no information" and the same process agreement. That's actually the healthiest possible version of uniformity, but it gives me nothing to distinguish anyone. I'm not going to manufacture a read out of nine identical answers, because there isn't one.

On the substance of the day, I want to be precise about where I stand.

First, Lucia's pre-committed check on Felix. I'll restate what I think it is and isn't. It's a genuinely good procedural move — publishing the target before the result removes the ability to retrofit a convenient choice, and I'd like to see that standard adopted generally. But Leo's point is the important one: the pre-commitment makes the check public property. If Lucia is the detective, the mafia know the result before we do and can pre-position their Day 2 behavior around it. So tomorrow's report should be read as one data point, not a resolution. I'll audit it the same way I audit everything else: does the stated order of checks match the stated plan, and does the result arrive in the shape that was promised?

Second, I want to endorse Felix's framing on the asymmetry. A no-elimination day costs tempo; a wrong elimination costs a villager, possibly a power role, permanently. With zero discriminating information on the table, abstaining is the defensible error. But I agree it should be a snapshot, not a default. If tomorrow produces a contradiction, a vote that doesn't match stated reasoning, or a night result, I'll vote on it — and I expect the same from everyone who spent today telling me they would.

Third, my own claim, for the record: no information, no role claim, no accusation. Consistent with what I said in turn one, I won't read anyone's silence about roles as guilt, and I won't be pressured into revealing anything myself just to look transparent.

What I'm actually watching for tonight and tomorrow: whether the vote pattern matches the stated standards. Almost every player alive has now explicitly committed to the same rule — votes must cite a claim, a reason, or a result. That's an unusually strong public record for Day 1, and it means tomorrow's votes carry more information than they otherwise would. Anyone who votes without citing one of those three things is contradicting their own stated standard, and that gap is exactly the kind of signal I said I'd weight most heavily. I'll be checking every voter's explanation against what they said today, including my own.

For now: no accusation, no vote rationale beyond abstention unless something concrete emerges before the vote. My claim remains no information, and my notes remain open for anyone to compare against the record tomorrow.

Maya, turn three. I’ll keep this brief because Day 1 has produced a clear record and I don’t want to add noise to it.

My position is unchanged. All nine of us gave no-information claims, and no one has produced a contradiction or a checkable accusation. A five-vote elimination built on that record would be a gamble, not evidence. I would abstain today unless something concrete emerges before the vote.

I accept Leo and Felix’s correction that no elimination is not free. It costs tempo and gives the mafia a night. But with zero discriminating information, the asymmetry still favors abstaining: tempo is recoverable, while a wrong elimination can permanently remove a villager or a power role. The key is that abstention should be a snapshot, not a default.

On Lucia’s soft investigative signal and pre-committed check on Felix, I’m treating it as a claim to audit, not proof. The pre-commitment is useful because it prevents retrofitting a target, but it also makes the intended check public. Tomorrow I want to compare the promised order and result shape against what is actually reported, and I want every vote explanation checked against the standard people stated today.

For now I have no accusation and no vote rationale beyond abstention unless the table produces something substantive.

Isha here, turn two.

I’ll keep this brief as the table has reached a very clear and sensible consensus. Everyone has placed their baseline on the record, and we have zero concrete evidence to justify eliminating anyone today. As several others have noted, while a no-elimination day does carry a tempo cost, pushing an uninformed elimination when five votes are needed is strictly worse—it risks losing a town member or an essential role on pure guesswork.

Regarding Lucia’s soft investigative signal and pre-commitment to inspect Felix: it creates a clean, falsifiable benchmark for Day 2. However, as Leo and Felix rightly pointed out, making that target public also gives the mafia complete information about where that check lands. We should be mindful tomorrow of how that shared awareness might shape night actions and subsequent claims.

At this point, we have established our expectations and audit trails. The true discriminating evidence will only arrive with night results and the vote accountability tomorrow. Unless someone brings new, verifiable information to light before the deadline, my vote today will be an abstention.

Zara, turn three. I'll keep this short, since the record is already clear and I don't want to dilute it.

My position is unchanged from my first two turns: no information, no role claim, no accusation. Nothing said since has produced a contradiction, a checkable claim, or a night result — the three things I said would move my vote. So my vote today remains an abstention, and that abstention is a snapshot, not a default. If tomorrow brings a contradiction, a vote that doesn't match stated reasoning, or a night result, I'll vote on it.

On Lucia's pre-committed check on Felix, I've already laid out my read: good procedure for auditability, but it makes the check public property. Tomorrow's report — target, answer, and order — should be compared against exactly what was promised, and read as one data point, not a resolution. If the report's shape doesn't match the commitment, that gap matters more than the report's content.

The one thing I'd underline as we close the day: nearly every player here has publicly committed to the same standard — votes must cite a claim, a reason, or a result. That's an unusually strong record, and it makes tomorrow's votes informative regardless of what the night brings. I'll be checking every voter's explanation against today's statements, including my own, and I'd encourage everyone else to do the same. Anyone who votes without citing one of those three things is contradicting a standard they themselves set, and that gap is the kind of signal I said I'd weight most heavily.

No accusation from me today. My claim remains no information, and my notes stay open for comparison tomorrow.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
All players abstained. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Felix is not mafia.
Nobody died during the night.
Day 2 begins.

No one died last night, so the first real event is the absence of a kill. That could mean the doctor guessed correctly, the mafia targeted someone protected, or something stranger happened. I don't think we can resolve that from the public result alone, and I won't pretend otherwise.

The one auditable promise on the table is Lucia's pre-committed check on Felix. Lucia, please give that report now in the exact shape you promised: confirm the target was Felix, state the answer you received, and confirm whether the order of checks matches what you said on Day 1. If you have any additional result, give it with the same target/answer/order detail. I will treat the report as a claim to compare against your prior commitment, not as automatic proof.

For my own position: I have no new role information and no accusation yet. I still think votes should cite a claim, a reason, or a result, and the no-death night makes the quality of that citation more important, not less.

Priya asked for the report in the exact shape I promised, so here it is, in writing, before any vote discussion. 1. Target: Felix. That is the name I pre-committed to on Day 1, and it is the name I checked on the night of Day 1. It is the first and only check I have made. 2. Answer: Felix is NOT mafia. 3. Order: my first check was Felix, on the first night. That matches my Day 1 commitment exactly — same target, same night, no substitutions, no retroactive changes. I told you I would report clean results too; this is a clean result, and I am publishing it even though it names no suspect, because a record that only names suspects is a hit list, not a record. On my role, I will state it plainly rather than leave it ambiguous: I am the detective. I said on Day 1 that I had a capacity to check people and intended to use it, and I have now attached a result to that capacity as I said I would. I am making the claim so you can audit it against the night. If I am lying, then a second checker exists who will produce a different report, and the contradiction itself becomes evidence. If I am telling the truth, then the record is now on the table with a shape anyone can compare. What this does and does not tell us: it tells us Felix is a town player. It does not tell us whether Felix is the doctor, a villager, or anything else, and it does not clear anyone else. Anyone reading a clean check on Felix as a general exculpation should stop — it covers one name only. On the night itself: nobody died. That is consistent with a doctor protecting the mafia's target, and it is consistent with a mafia that chose not to kill. I cannot resolve which from the public result, and I won't pretend to. It is not evidence for or against any name. One honest note about procedure, and I am flagging it rather than letting it be noticed later. On Day 1 I pre-announced my target because retro-fitting a target after seeing the answer would make the report worthless. I still hold to that: every check I report will name the target, the answer, and the order of checks, so it can be checked against my stated plan. What I will change is the daily pre-announcement of the next target, because Leo and Felix correctly identified that a public pre-commitment hands the mafia my next check and my role in one move. The auditability I care about comes from the published order of checks, not from announcing them a day early. My position today: no accusation, no vote on anyone on the current record. Felix is confirmed town by my check. If someone wants to accuse Felix today, I will say plainly that it contradicts my published result, and I would

Arjun here. Lucia has now published a result: she checked Felix on the first night and got not mafia. I'm treating that as a claim, not proof, but it matches her Day 1 pre-commitment, so it's the strongest checkable information we have. It clears Felix only. It does not clear anyone else, and it doesn't tell us whether Felix is the doctor or a villager. Nobody died last night, which is consistent with a doctor protecting a target, or with the mafia choosing not to kill. Neither reading points to a name yet, so I still have no accusation and no vote on the current record. Lucia, your message cut off at 'I would', right where you were explaining how you'd respond if someone accused Felix today. Please finish that point so we have your full position on Felix before votes.

Lucia, turn two. Arjun, first: your message cut off mid-sentence, so let me finish it exactly. If someone accuses Felix today, I will say plainly that it contradicts my published result, and I will treat that accusation as information about the accuser rather than about Felix. Felix is confirmed town by my check on the first night, and a clean check covers exactly one name. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
